--- jupyter: stats --- # Python Basics for `sklearn` This note introduces only the Python syntax needed for the rest of these notes. The goal is not to cover Python as a full programming language. The goal is to make code using `numpy`, `matplotlib`, and `sklearn` readable. ## Running Python Code A Python code chunk looks like this: ::: {.cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} # This is a comment x = 10 # assignment uses = a, b = 2, 3 a + b # last expression is automatically displayed ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 5 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Notebook 1. When a code cell is executed, the value of the last expression is automatically displayed. Any explicit output commands, such as `print()`, will also produce output. 2. Use `#` comments only for short notes that help explain the code. Detailed explanations and discussion should be written in Markdown cells, where they are easier to read and maintain. ::: ### Indentation Python uses indentation to mark code blocks. R uses braces `{}`; Python uses indentation. For example, a `for` loop: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} for k in [1, 3, 5]: print(k) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 3 5 ``` ::: ::: The indented block belongs to the loop. These notes use loops only when they are helpful for plotting or comparing models. ### `if` and `for` The logic of `if` statements and `for` loops is straightforward. When using them, pay attention to indentation. A colon `:` indicates the beginning of an indented code block. ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = 1 if x == 2: print('good') else: print('not good') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` not good ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} for k in range(4): print(k) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 0 1 2 3 ``` ::: ::: ### Functions and Objects This is not an object-oriented programming course, so don't worry too much about the details. The important idea is the distinction between a function, a class, and an object created from a class. - Function: performs an action and returns a result. Called with parentheses: `round(3.14, 2)` - Class: a blueprint for creating objects. - Object: stores information and provides methods. Accessed with a dot: `object.method()` Example in scikit-learn: ```python model = LinearRegression() ``` Here - `LinearRegression` is the class; - `LinearRegression()` creates a linear regression model object; - the object is assigned to the variable `model`. ```python model.fit(X_train, y_train) coef = model.coef_ ``` Here - `fit()` is method; - `coef_` stores information about the fitted model; - methods are called using `object.method(...)`; - stored information is accessed using `object.attribute`. In almost all `scikit-learn` code, you should work with objects rather than classes. A common mistake is to pass a class where an object is required. ```python pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler, LinearRegression) # wrong pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression()) # correct ``` The same idea applies to most `scikit-learn` components, including transformers, models, and pipelines. In general, if something is used as a step in a pipeline, you should create an object by adding `()`. ::: {.callout-caution} ## `.` (Dot) The meaning of `.` is different in Python and R. - In Python, `.` is used to access methods and attributes of an object. ```python model.fit(X, y) model.coef_ ``` - In R, `.` is usually just part of a variable or function name. ```r my.variable <- 1 ``` Do not interpret dots in R names as object access. ::: ### Importing Packages Python packages are loaded with `import`. The usual imports in these notes are: ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ``` ::: The names on the right are aliases: - `numpy` is used as `np`; - `pandas` is used as `pd`; - `matplotlib.pyplot` is used as `plt`. After importing a package this way, you access its functions using the package name, e.g. - `np.array([1, 2, 3])` - `pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3]})` - `plt.plot([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6])` ::: {.callout-note} When a package is imported with `import ... as ...`, you must use the alias to access its functions and classes instead of the original name. ::: Sometimes only specific functions or classes are imported. ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split ``` ::: These objects can then be used directly. ::: {.cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} model = LinearRegression() ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} After `from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression`, you may use `LinearRegression()` directly, but other objects from `sklearn.linear_model` are not automatically imported. ::: ## Data structure ### Basic Objects Python has several basic data types. ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = 3 # integer y = 2.5 # float name = "tree" # string flag = True # Boolean ``` ::: Use `type()` to check the type of an object. ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} type(y) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` float ``` ::: ::: Python is case-sensitive. `x` and `X` are different objects. ### Lists A list is an **ordered collection** of objects. Lists are commonly used to store variable names, column names, or collections of parameter values. | Purpose | Example | Explanation | | ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ | | Create a list | `features = ["age", "income", "education"]` | Creates a list containing three strings. | | Access the first element | `features[0]` | Returns `"age"`. Python indexing starts at `0`. | | Access the last element | `features[-1]` | Returns `"education"`. Negative indices count from the end. | | Select several elements | `features[0:2]` | Returns `["age", "income"]`. The stop index is not included. | | Add an element | `features.append("gender")` | Adds `"gender"` to the end of the list. | | Count elements | `len(features)` | Returns the number of elements in the list. | ::: {.callout-note} Unlike R, Python uses zero-based indexing, so the first element has index `0`. ::: ### Dictionaries A dictionary stores **key-value pairs**. It is similar to a named list in R and is commonly used to store settings, options, and model parameters. | Purpose | Example | Explanation | | --------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | | Create a dictionary | `params = {"n_neighbors": 5, "weights": "uniform"}` | Creates a dictionary with two keys and their values. | | Access a value | `params["n_neighbors"]` | Returns `5`. | | Add or update a value | `params["metric"] = "euclidean"` | Adds a new key-value pair or updates an existing one. | | Count entries | `len(params)` | Returns the number of key-value pairs. | | Store model settings | `{"max_depth": 3, "min_samples_leaf": 5}` | A common use in machine learning. | | Store parameter grids | `{"max_depth": [2,3,4]}` | Often used when tuning hyperparameters. | A typical parameter grid in `scikit-learn` looks like: ```python param_grid = { "max_depth": [2, 3, 4], "min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10], } ``` For pipelines, parameter names often use two underscores: ```python param_grid = { "model__C": [0.1, 1, 10], } ``` ::: {.callout-note} In a pipeline, a parameter name of the form `step__parameter` refers to a parameter inside a specific pipeline step. For example, `model__C` means the parameter `C` of the pipeline step named `"model"`. More terminologies will be discussed in related sections. ::: ## `numpy.array` The most important data structure for numerical computation in Python is `numpy.array`. ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array([1, 2, 3, 4]) ``` ::: ::: Arrays have a shape and a dimension. ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(x.shape) print(x.ndim) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (4,) 1 ``` ::: ::: So `x` is a 1D array containing 4 elements. ### 2D Arrays A 2D array is similar to a matrix. ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = np.array([ [1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6] ]) X ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ``` array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(X.shape) print(X.ndim) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (3, 2) 2 ``` ::: ::: Here `X` is a 2D array with 3 rows and 2 columns. ### Indexing Use `[row, column]` indexing. ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} X[0, 1] # row 0, column 1 X[:, 0] # first column X[1, :] # second row ``` ::: The symbol `:` means "all indices" along that axis. Slicing can select ranges. ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} X[0:2, 1] # first 2 rows, column 1 X[0, 0:2] # row 0, first 2 columns X[0:2, 0:2] # upper-left 2x2 block ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} `X[:, 0]` returns a 1D array with shape `(n,)`, not a column vector. To obtain a column vector, use ::: {.cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} X[:, [0]] # or X[:, 0].reshape(-1, 1) ``` ::: which both have shape `(n, 1)`. ::: ### Common Operations {#sec-common_operations} Arrays support vectorized arithmetic. ::: {.cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} x + 1 x * 2 np.mean(x) ``` ::: Operations are applied elementwise. There are two special operations that is worth mentioning. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Matrix multiplication There are several ways to perform matrix multiplication in NumPy. Here we introduce the `@` operator because it has the simplest syntax. ::: {.cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) y = np.array([1, 2]) X @ y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ``` array([ 5, 11, 17]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) y = np.array([1, 2]).reshape(-1, 1) X @ y ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ``` array([[ 5], [11], [17]]) ``` ::: ::: Note that the result depends on the dimensions of the inputs. NumPy automatically applies the appropriate matrix multiplication rule based on the shapes of the arrays. - In the first example, `y` is a one-dimensional array with shape `(2,)`, so the result is also one-dimensional with shape `(3,)`. - In the second example, `y` is a column vector with shape `(2,1)`, so the result is a two-dimensional array with shape `(3,1)`. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Broadcasting Broadcasting is a NumPy mechanism that allows arithmetic operations between arrays of different shapes. Instead of explicitly copying data, NumPy automatically expands arrays along dimensions of size 1 when the shapes are compatible. A common example is arithmetic between an array and a scalar: ::: {.cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np X = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) X + 10 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ``` array([[11, 12], [13, 14], [15, 16]]) ``` ::: ::: The scalar is automatically applied to every element of the array. Broadcasting can also be used to compute pairwise differences efficiently. ::: {.cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np X1 = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) X2 = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]]) d = X1[:, None] - X2[None, :] d ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ``` array([[[ 0, 0], [-2, -2]], [[ 2, 2], [ 0, 0]]]) ``` ::: ::: `None` inserts a new dimension at the specified location. Therefore `X1[:, None]` has shape `(2,1,2)` while `X2[None, :]` has shape `(1,2,2)`. NumPy automatically broadcasts these arrays to shape `(2, 2, 2)` and computes all pairwise differences at once. In this example, each row of `X1` is subtracted from each row of `X2`. The result satisfies `d[i, j] = X1[i] - X2[j]` for all valid indices `i` and `j`. This technique is frequently used when computing distance matrices in machine learning algorithms. ::: ### Axis-wise Many functions accept an `axis=` argument. ::: {.cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} X # show X ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ``` array([[1, 2], [3, 4], [5, 6]]) ``` ::: ::: Computes the sum across rows: ::: {.cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.sum(axis=0) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ``` array([ 9, 12]) ``` ::: ::: Computes the mean across columns: ::: {.cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.mean(axis=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` array([1.5, 3.5, 5.5]) ``` ::: ::: A useful rule: - `axis=0`: operate down rows (one result per column) - `axis=1`: operate across columns (one result per row) ### Reshaping A 1D array can be converted into a matrix. Consider a 1D array ::: {.cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) ``` ::: To create a column vector: ::: {.cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} x.reshape(-1, 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ``` array([[1], [2], [3], [4]]) ``` ::: ::: To create a row vector: ::: {.cell execution_count=27} ``` {.python .cell-code} x.reshape(1, -1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ``` array([[1, 2, 3, 4]]) ``` ::: ::: The value `-1` means "infer this dimension automatically." A common pattern is ::: {.cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} test_x = np.linspace(0, 1, 101).reshape(-1, 1) ``` ::: On the other side, to flatten an array back to 1D: ::: {.cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.reshape(-1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ``` array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]) ``` ::: ::: `NumPy` reads entries row by row and produces a one-dimensional array. ::: {.callout-tip} Other flattening methods include `.ravel()` and `.flatten()`. The difference is about how copy-and-view is handled. We mainly use `.reshape(-1)` because it makes the resulting shape explicit. ::: ::: {.callout-note} One common source of bugs in statistical learning is using arrays with incorrect shapes. In `scikit-learn`, predictors `X` are usually stored as a 2D array and responses `y` as a 1D array. Other libraries may use different conventions, and the required shapes often depend on the specific model or loss function. When shape-related errors occur, always check the documentation of the library you are using. ::: ### Arrays versus Lists Lists are general-purpose containers, and its addition concatenates. For example ::: {.cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} [1, 2, 3] + [4, 5, 6] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] ``` ::: ::: Arrays are designed for numerical computation. Its operations are align with the regular math operations. Therefore for numerical work and machine learning, use `numpy.array` whenever possible. ## Random Numbers These notes often use `numpy` random number generators for simulation. ::: {.cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(1) x = rng.normal(size=5) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ``` array([ 0.34558419, 0.82161814, 0.33043708, -1.30315723, 0.90535587]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} The number `1` is a seed. It makes the random output reproducible. On a single machine, if the seed is fixed the results are supposed to be the same. You may choose any number as the seed. You may use the same seed when you want to see the same result. ::: Some common random functions are: ::: {.cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng.normal(loc=0, scale=1, size=5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ``` array([ 0.44637457, -0.53695324, 0.5811181 , 0.3645724 , 0.2941325 ]) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng.uniform(0, 1, size=5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=27} ``` array([0.75351311, 0.53814331, 0.32973172, 0.7884287 , 0.30319483]) ``` ::: ::: For a two-dimensional predictor matrix: ::: {.cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = rng.normal(size=(10, 3)) X.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=28} ``` (10, 3) ``` ::: ::: ## `pandas` `pandas` can be treated as a wrapper of `numpy.array` which make it more readable. The complete `pandas` is very complicated. Here we only mention a few very important concepts. To import `pandas`, in most cases we set `pd` as its alias. ::: {.cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd ``` ::: ### `DataFrame` and `Series` In `pandas`, `DataFrame` is the 2D data table, and `Series` is the 1D column. There are many ways to create a `DataFrame`. Here we focus on one of them, that is to convert a `dict` into a `DataFrame`. ::: {.cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} results = { 'round': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'score': [0.22, 0.33, 0.44, 0.55, 0.66], 'mse': [0.12, 0.11, 0.10, 0.09, 0.08] } df_res = pd.DataFrame(results) df_res ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ```{=html}
round score mse
0 1 0.22 0.12
1 2 0.33 0.11
2 3 0.44 0.10
3 4 0.55 0.09
4 5 0.66 0.08
``` ::: ::: A single column is returned as a `Series`. ::: {.cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_res['score'] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=31} ``` 0 0.22 1 0.33 2 0.44 3 0.55 4 0.66 Name: score, dtype: float64 ``` ::: ::: Notice that this is similar to `numpy` indexing. Selecting a single column by name returns a 1D object. If we instead pass a list of column names, even if the list contains only one column (e.g. `['score']` below), the result is a 2D `DataFrame`. ::: {.cell execution_count=38} ``` {.python .cell-code} df_res[['score']] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=32} ```{=html}
score
0 0.22
1 0.33
2 0.44
3 0.55
4 0.66
``` ::: ::: This behavior is analogous to the difference between `X[:, 0]` and `X[:, [0]]` for a `numpy` array: - `df_res["score"]` returns a `Series` (1D) - `df_res[["score"]]` returns a `DataFrame` (2D) - `X[:, 0]` returns a 1D array - `X[:, [0]]` returns a 2D array ### Read and write files In `scikit-learn`, predictors and responses can be stored either as `numpy` arrays or as `pandas` objects. Throughout this course, many examples use `numpy`, but most code works equally well with `pandas` data structures. When working with external datasets, a common workflow is: 1. Read the data into a `DataFrame`. 2. Perform data cleaning and preprocessing. 3. Extract predictors and responses. 4. Fit a statistical learning model. Two of the most common tabular file formats are CSV files and Excel spreadsheets. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## CSV CSV stands for comma-separated values. A CSV file is a plain-text file that stores tabular data using a separator between columns. Common separators include: - `,` (comma) - `;` (semicolon) - `\t` (tab) Consider the following file [`example.csv`](example.csv). ``` round score mse 1 0.220000 0.120000 2 0.330000 0.110000 3 0.440000 0.100000 4 0.550000 0.090000 5 0.660000 0.080000 ``` In Python we could use `pd.read_csv()` to read it. ::: {.cell execution_count=39} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd df = pd.read_csv('example.csv') df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=33} ```{=html}
round\tscore\tmse
0 1\t0.220000\t0.120000
1 2\t0.330000\t0.110000
2 3\t0.440000\t0.100000
3 4\t0.550000\t0.090000
4 5\t0.660000\t0.080000
``` ::: ::: The result is incorrect because this file uses tab characters (`\t`) rather than commas as separators. Specify the separator explicitly: ::: {.cell execution_count=40} ``` {.python .cell-code} df = pd.read_csv('example.csv', sep='\t') df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=34} ```{=html}
round score mse
0 1 0.22 0.12
1 2 0.33 0.11
2 3 0.44 0.10
3 4 0.55 0.09
4 5 0.66 0.08
``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Excel Excel spreadsheets can be read using `pd.read_excel()`. We provide the [`exmaple.xlsx`](example.xlsx) as an example. ::: {.cell execution_count=41} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd df = pd.read_excel('example.xlsx') df ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=35} ```{=html}
round score mse
0 1 0.22 0.12
1 2 0.33 0.11
2 3 0.44 0.10
3 4 0.55 0.09
4 5 0.66 0.08
``` ::: ::: Unlike CSV files, Excel files are stored in a binary format. Therefore, `pandas` requires an additional package called an engine to read and write them. The most commonly used engine is `openpyxl`. ```bash uv add openpyxl ``` Although not provided in the toml file, `openpyxl` was added to our environment as an example in the introduction. If you didn't add it at that time you may add it now. ::: Writing files is similar to reading files. The main difference is that writing starts from an existing `DataFrame` instead of starting from `pd`. ```python df.to_csv('example2.csv') df.to_excel('example2.xlsx') ``` ### Relative paths In this course, always use relative paths when reading or writing files. A relative path starts from the current working directory rather than from the root of the file system. Suppose your working directory is ```text C:/Users/WDAGUtilityAccount/Project/ ``` and you have the following structure: ```text Project/ ├── example.csv └── foldername/ ``` Then you can read and write files using: ```python df = pd.read_csv("example.csv") df.to_csv("foldername/result.csv") ``` Notice that neither path begins with a drive name such as `C:` or `D:`. If your files are stored outside the working directory, **copy them into the working directory** before reading them. ::: {.callout-note} Although absolute paths such as ```python pd.read_csv("D:/Files/example.csv") ``` often work on your own computer, they may fail on another computer because the file locations are different. Using relative paths makes your code more portable and easier to share. ::: ## `matplotlib` Basics These notes use only basic `matplotlib`. The standard import is: ::: {.cell execution_count=42} ``` {.python .cell-code} import matplotlib.pyplot as plt ``` ::: We provide some code examples here. Most of the commands are straightforward. Please check the [official document](https://matplotlib.org/) if you need more details. ### Scatter Plot ::: {.cell execution_count=43} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4]) y = np.array([1.1, 2.0, 2.8, 4.2]) plt.scatter(x, y) plt.xlabel("x") plt.ylabel("y") plt.title("Scatter Plot"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python_files/figure-pdf/cell-44-output-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: ### Line Plot ::: {.cell execution_count=44} ``` {.python .cell-code} x_grid = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200) y_grid = np.sin(x_grid) plt.plot(x_grid, y_grid) plt.xlabel("x") plt.ylabel("sin(x)") plt.title("Line Plot"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python_files/figure-pdf/cell-45-output-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: ### Scatter and Line Together ::: {.cell execution_count=45} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(1) x = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, size=30) y = np.sin(x) + rng.normal(scale=0.2, size=30) x_grid = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200) plt.scatter(x, y, facecolors="none", edgecolors="black") plt.plot(x_grid, np.sin(x_grid), color="C1") plt.xlabel("x") plt.ylabel("y") plt.title("Data and Curve"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python_files/figure-pdf/cell-46-output-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: This pattern appears often when we plot data points and a fitted curve. ### Multiple Plots Use `plt.subplots` for multiple panels. ::: {.cell execution_count=46} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4)) axs[0].scatter(x, y) axs[0].set_title("scatter") axs[1].plot(x_grid, np.sin(x_grid)) axs[1].set_title("line"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python_files/figure-pdf/cell-47-output-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} Notice that when using an axes object, many plotting commands have different names. For example, `plt.title()` becomes `ax.set_title()`. Therefore, you cannot always replace `plt` with `ax` directly. For details, consult the official documentation. ::: ### Histograms ::: {.cell execution_count=47} ``` {.python .cell-code} z = rng.normal(size=200) plt.hist(z, bins=20, edgecolor="black") plt.xlabel("z") plt.ylabel("count") plt.title("Histogram"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](python_files/figure-pdf/cell-48-output-1.pdf){fig-pos='H'} ::: ::: ## Common Errors ### One-Dimensional `X` The most common error is passing a one-dimensional predictor array to `sklearn`. | Bad | Good | |------|------| | `x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4])`
`model.fit(x, y)` | `X = x.reshape(-1, 1)`
`model.fit(X, y)` | ### Class Name versus Model Object Another common mistake is confusing an `sklearn` class with an object created from that class. For example, `DecisionTreeClassifier` is the class itself. | Wrong | Right | |------|------| | `model = DecisionTreeClassifier`
`model.fit(X_train, y_train)` | `model = DecisionTreeClassifier()`
`model.fit(X_train, y_train)` | ### Mixing Lists and Arrays Use arrays for elementwise numerical operations. ::: {.cell execution_count=48} ``` {.python .cell-code} [1, 2, 3] * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=42} ``` [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] ``` ::: ::: Plain lists do not always behave like numerical vectors. ::: {.cell execution_count=49} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np np.array([1, 2, 3]) * 2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=43} ``` array([2, 4, 6]) ``` ::: :::
